title: Dissipation as a Resource
intro: A closed quantum system never forgets its initial state, so a quantum reservoir needs some non-unitary ingredient (a reset, a measurement or genuine dissipation) to have the echo state property. How much dissipation, of which kind, and where it enters decide both whether the reservoir works and how long its memory is.

blocks.text: What you need first

The reset-injection model of The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir), the encodings of Input Encoding (#/qrc/models/input-encoding) (especially the drive encoding), and the idea of a contraction from The Echo State Property (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-property). From the open-systems chapter: Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels) (a quantum channel as a map on density matrices) and Lindblad Dynamics (#/qrc/open-systems/lindblad-dynamics) (damping and dephasing as a rate equation). The key facts are restated where used.
What you will be able to do

items: Show that a unitary reservoir has no echo state property and that a unitary reservoir started in the maximally mixed state never responds to its input.
Name three sources of dissipation (reset, measurement, environmental noise) and say which are available on a given platform.
Turn a measured trace distance into a per-step contraction factor and a washout length.
Explain why unital noise (depolarising) alone cannot make a reservoir work, while non-unital noise (amplitude damping) can.
Choose a dissipation strength from the memory a task needs, and read a sweep of memory against loss rate.

blocks.text: Why a closed quantum system cannot be a reservoir
Why we need it

A classical reservoir is useful because its state is a function of the recent inputs only: whatever the state was when you switched it on has faded away (the echo state property). Quantum mechanics seems to rule this out at the first step. Closed quantum evolution is reversible: from the state now you can compute the state at any earlier time. A reversible system cannot forget. So how can a quantum system be a reservoir at all?
The idea in plain words

It cannot, unless something irreversible happens. A bell that rings forever remembers every strike; a bell with a damping pad forgets old strikes at a rate set by the pad. Reversible dynamics is the bell without the pad: two different starting states stay exactly as different as they started, however long you drive them with the same input.
The maths, step by step

Write one input step as a map on density matrices, $\rho_k=\mathcal{T}_{s_k}(\rho_{k-1})$. The echo state property asks that two different initial states $\rho_0$ and $\sigma_0$ fed the same inputs become indistinguishable, in the sense that the trace norm of their difference, $\Vert\rho-\sigma\Vert_1=\sum_j\vert\lambda_j\vert$ (the sum of the absolute values of the eigenvalues of $\rho-\sigma$), goes to zero. Suppose every step is unitary, $\mathcal{T}_s(\rho)=U_s\rho U_s^\dagger$.

items: Step 1. The difference evolves the same way: $\mathcal{T}(\rho)-\mathcal{T}(\sigma)=U(\rho-\sigma)U^\dagger$.
Step 2. Conjugation by a unitary does not change eigenvalues: $U(\rho-\sigma)U^\dagger$ has the same eigenvalues as $\rho-\sigma$.
Step 3. So the trace norm is exactly conserved at every step: $\Vert U(\rho-\sigma)U^\dagger\Vert_1=\Vert\rho-\sigma\Vert_1$. The reservoir remembers its initial condition forever, with full weight.

blocks.text: There is a second, quieter failure. The maximally mixed state $I/D$ (where $D=2^n$) satisfies $U(I/D)U^\dagger=I/D$ for every unitary $U$: it is a fixed point of every unitary channel. A reservoir started there (the natural 'thermal' start) never moves, and every feature $\langle Z_i\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(Z_i)/D=0$ whatever the input. The input has to enter through something that changes the spectrum of $\rho$ (its eigenvalues), not just its basis.

So a working quantum reservoir needs a step that is strictly contractive (see Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points)): $\Vert\mathcal{T}_s(\rho)-\mathcal{T}_s(\sigma)\Vert_1\le c\,\Vert\rho-\sigma\Vert_1$ with $c<1$ for every input, or at least a composition of steps that contracts. Chen and Nurdin made a condition of this kind central to their universality result: for every input, the step map restricted to traceless operators must have induced Hilbert-Schmidt norm at most $1-\epsilon$, which makes any two initial states converge. Convergent dissipative systems of this kind, combined as non-interacting subsystems and read out by a polynomial in the single-qubit expectations, can approximate any fading-memory input-output map arbitrarily well.

blocks.title: Check yourself: the frozen mixed state
blocks.text: A reservoir with unitary input encoding $\rho\mapsto R(s)\rho R(s)^\dagger$ and unitary evolution starts in $\rho_0=I/D$. Show that its features never depend on the input, and name a change that fixes it.
blocks.hint: What does a unitary do to the identity matrix?
solution: $R(I/D)R^\dagger=I/D$ and $U(I/D)U^\dagger=I/D$ for any unitaries, so $\rho_k=I/D$ for all $k$.
Then $\langle Z_i\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(Z_i)/D=0$ for every step and input.
Fixes: add a reset or amplitude damping, which moves $I/D$ toward an input-dependent state. (Starting in a pure state alone does not help: the reservoir then moves, but never forgets its start.)

blocks.text: Three places dissipation can come from

items: Reset injection. The Fujii-Nakajima scheme replaces qubit 1 by a fresh state at each step: $\rho\mapsto\vert\psi(s)\rangle\langle\psi(s)\vert\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_1\rho$. Tracing out the old qubit throws away information each step; this alone makes the map contractive on the remaining qubits once the Hamiltonian spreads information from the rest onto qubit 1. This is the model of The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir).

Measurement. A projective or weak measurement followed by discarding the outcome is a dephasing channel; keeping the outcome and conditioning on it is a different, stochastic map. Either way it removes coherence and gives contraction; see Measurement (#/qrc/open-systems/measurement) and Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action).

Engineered or natural environmental noise. Amplitude damping (energy relaxation at rate $\gamma=1/T_1$), dephasing (rate $1/T_\phi$) and depolarisation. On hardware this noise is free; in simulation it is a Lindblad term. Here the reservoir can encode the input unitarily (a rotation, a field) and still have the echo state property.

blocks.text: Which is right depends on the platform. A gate-based processor can reset qubits but the reset is slow; an NMR ensemble has relaxation but no reset; a photonic loop has loss. The page's remaining sections use the third kind because it is the cleanest to analyse, and then return to the others.
A model: unitary encoding plus amplitude damping
The setup

Take the spin reservoir $H=\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}X_iX_j+h\sum_iZ_i$ with $J_{ij}\sim U[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$ and $h=1$ on $n=4$ qubits. Encode the input unitarily, with no reset: rotate qubit 1 by $R_y(\pi s_k)$. Then evolve for $\Delta t=3$ under the Lindblad equation with amplitude damping on every qubit,

Read the symbols: $\sigma_i^-=\vert0\rangle\langle1\vert$ on qubit $i$ lowers the qubit from $\vert1\rangle$ to $\vert0\rangle$ (in our convention $Z\vert0\rangle=+\vert0\rangle$, so damping drives $\langle Z\rangle$ toward $+1$), $\gamma$ is the loss rate, and $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$. The first term is the unitary evolution, the second the loss. For one qubit this gives the simple results $\langle Z\rangle(t)=1-(1-\langle Z\rangle_0)e^{-\gamma t}$ for the population and $e^{-\gamma t/2}$ for the coherence. With $\gamma=0.3$ and $\Delta t=3$: $e^{-0.9}=0.407$ of a deviation from the ground state survives each step.

The step map is $\mathcal{T}_s=e^{\mathcal{L}\Delta t}\circ\mathcal{R}_s$: a unitary rotation followed by a fixed contractive semigroup ($\mathcal{L}$ is the generator, the whole right-hand side above). The program sweeps $\gamma$ and reports two numbers. One is the linear memory capacity for delays 1 to 10. The other is the trace distance after 60 steps between copies started in $\vert0000\rangle$ and $\vert1111\rangle$, which measures whether the echo state property holds.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm

n = 4; D = 2 ** n
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1., -1]); Sm = np.array([[0, 1], [0, 0]])  # sigma^- = |0><1|
def op(o, i):
    m = np.array([[1.]])
    for k in range(n): m = np.kron(m, o if k == i else np.eye(2))
    return m
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
H = sum(rng.uniform(-.5, .5) * op(X, i) @ op(X, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n))
H = H + sum(1.0 * op(Z, i) for i in range(n))
I = np.eye(D)
def liouvillian(gamma):
    """Lindblad generator with amplitude damping at rate gamma on every qubit (column-stacked vec)."""
    L = -1j * (np.kron(I, H) - np.kron(H.T, I))
    for i in range(n):
        c = np.sqrt(gamma) * op(Sm, i); cdc = c.conj().T @ c
        L += np.kron(c.conj(), c) - 0.5 * np.kron(I, cdc) - 0.5 * np.kron(cdc.T, I)
    return L
def ry(t): return np.array([[np.cos(t / 2), -np.sin(t / 2)], [np.sin(t / 2), np.cos(t / 2)]])
def run(s, gamma, dt=3.0, rho0=None):
    P = expm(liouvillian(gamma) * dt)
    rho = np.eye(D) / D if rho0 is None else rho0
    Zd = [np.diag(op(Z, i)) for i in range(n)]; feats = []
    for x in s:
        R = op(ry(np.pi * x), 0)            # unitary input: rotate qubit 1 by pi*s (no reset)
        rho = R @ rho @ R.T
        rho = (P @ rho.reshape(-1, order="F")).reshape(D, D, order="F")
        feats.append([np.real(z @ np.diag(rho)) for z in Zd])
    return np.array(feats), rho
def r2(p, y):
    if np.std(p) < 1e-12: return 0.0       # constant features carry no information
    return np.corrcoef(p, y)[0, 1] ** 2
def mc(F, s, w0=100, tr=600, dmax=10):
    A = np.hstack([F, np.ones((len(F), 1))]); out = 0
    for d in range(1, dmax + 1):
        w = np.linalg.lstsq(A[w0:w0 + tr], s[w0 - d:w0 + tr - d], rcond=1e-8)[0]
        out += r2(A[w0 + tr:] @ w, s[w0 + tr - d:len(s) - d])
    return out
s = np.random.default_rng(5).uniform(0, 1, 1000)
up = np.zeros((D, D)); up[0, 0] = 1; dn = np.zeros((D, D)); dn[-1, -1] = 1
for g in [0.0, 0.003, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 3.0]:
    F, _ = run(s, g)
    _, ra = run(s[:60], g, rho0=up); _, rb = run(s[:60], g, rho0=dn)   # echo-state check
    td = 0.5 * np.abs(np.linalg.eigvalsh(ra - rb)).sum()
    print(f"gamma={g:<6} MC(1..10)={mc(F, s):.2f}  trace distance after 60 steps={td:.1e}")

blocks.text: Output of that run:

items: $\gamma=0$: MC $=0.00$, trace distance $1.0$. Unitary: no echo state property, and from $I/D$ nothing moves at all.
$\gamma=0.003$: MC $0.36$, distance $0.39$. It contracts, but far too slowly: 60 steps are not a washout.
$\gamma=0.03$: MC $1.01$, distance $1.8\times10^{-4}$.
$\gamma=0.1$: MC $1.33$, distance $1.1\times10^{-9}$.
$\gamma=0.3$: MC $1.57$, distance at machine precision ($4\times10^{-16}$). Best of the sweep.
$\gamma=3$: MC $0.05$. Each step's input is wiped out before the next arrives: $e^{-\gamma\Delta t}=e^{-9}\approx1.2\times10^{-4}$ survives.

blocks.text: The sweep shows the general lesson, in line with Sannia et al., who found that tuning local loss rates boosts reservoir performance: performance is non-monotonic in the dissipation rate. Too little and the reservoir neither forgets its initial state nor settles to an input-determined trajectory; too much and it forgets the inputs too. The optimum sits where the contraction time (a few steps) matches the memory the task needs. The memory is set by the dissipation, not by the Hilbert-space dimension: here MC stays below 2 although the classical bound is the number of features.
Turning a trace distance into a washout
Suppose the distance shrinks by the same factor every step. From the $\gamma=0.03$ row, $1.8\times10^{-4}$ after 60 steps:

items: Step 3. So discard about 100 steps before training. If the washout is shorter, the training data still contain the starting state's imprint and the readout learns it.

blocks.text: Rule of thumb: the per-step contraction factor $c$ sets the memory horizon. Inputs older than about $1/\ln(1/c)$ steps are attenuated by $e$ or more (for $c=0.866$, about 7 steps). Tune $\gamma\Delta t$ (or the reset rate, or the measurement strength) until that horizon covers the delays your task needs, then stop.

blocks.title: Check yourself: washout from a measured contraction
blocks.text: Two copies of a reservoir started in orthogonal states have trace distance 1 at the start and $1.8\times10^{-4}$ after 60 steps. Assuming geometric contraction, what is the per-step factor, and how many steps bring the distance to $10^{-6}$?
Where the nonlinearity comes from

All the maps above are linear in $\rho$. The nonlinearity in the input-output map comes from two places: the encoding $s\mapsto\rho(s)$ (here $R_y(\pi s)$ makes the state depend on $\cos\pi s$ and $\sin\pi s$), and the products of encodings that build up over successive steps, because $\rho_k$ is multilinear in the encoded inputs $\rho(s_k),\rho(s_{k-1}),\dots$ when each enters through a tensor or rotation. Dissipation does not add nonlinearity in $s$; it decides which of these products survive. A strongly dissipative reservoir keeps only short products (low-order, short-memory terms); a weakly dissipative one keeps long ones but cannot separate them from the initial condition. Sannia et al. show that continuous local losses in spin-network reservoirs can take over the role of the discontinuous reset maps of earlier proposals, improve linear and nonlinear memory tasks and chaotic-series forecasting, and still form a universal class.
Why unital noise is not enough
Why we need it

On a real device the noise is already there, so can we simply rely on it? It depends on the kind. A noise channel is unital if it maps the maximally mixed state to itself; depolarising and dephasing are unital, amplitude damping is not.
Worked by hand: depolarising

The global depolarising channel $\mathcal{D}_p(\rho)=(1-p)\rho+p\,I/D$ maps a difference $\rho-\sigma$ to $(1-p)(\rho-\sigma)$ (the $I/D$ parts cancel). So the trace distance falls by exactly $1-p$ per step. It also shrinks every traceless observable's expectation by $1-p$: memory and signal decay together.

items: Take $p=0.05$. Per step factor $0.95$.
Half-life of the trace distance: $N=\ln2/(-\ln0.95)=0.693/0.0513=13.5$ steps.
A feature $\langle Z_1\rangle$ set to $0.8$ by the last input and not moved since is $0.4$ after 13.5 steps and $0.2$ after 27.

blocks.text: The program below tests this in the full reservoir. Same Hamiltonian, same unitary encoding $R_y(\pi s)$, starting in $I/D$, $\Delta t=3$: once with amplitude damping at $\gamma=0.3$ (which worked above) and twice with only global depolarising noise.

import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm

n = 4; D = 2 ** n
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1., -1]); Sm = np.array([[0, 1], [0, 0]])  # sigma^- = |0><1|
def op(o, i):
    m = np.array([[1.]])
    for k in range(n): m = np.kron(m, o if k == i else np.eye(2))
    return m
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
H = sum(rng.uniform(-.5, .5) * op(X, i) @ op(X, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n))
H = H + sum(1.0 * op(Z, i) for i in range(n))
I = np.eye(D)
def liouvillian(gamma):
    """Lindblad generator with amplitude damping at rate gamma on every qubit (column-stacked vec)."""
    L = -1j * (np.kron(I, H) - np.kron(H.T, I))
    for i in range(n):
        c = np.sqrt(gamma) * op(Sm, i); cdc = c.conj().T @ c
        L += np.kron(c.conj(), c) - 0.5 * np.kron(I, cdc) - 0.5 * np.kron(cdc.T, I)
    return L
def ry(t): return np.array([[np.cos(t / 2), -np.sin(t / 2)], [np.sin(t / 2), np.cos(t / 2)]])
def run(s, gamma, dt=3.0, rho0=None):
    P = expm(liouvillian(gamma) * dt)
    rho = np.eye(D) / D if rho0 is None else rho0
    Zd = [np.diag(op(Z, i)) for i in range(n)]; feats = []
    for x in s:
        R = op(ry(np.pi * x), 0)            # unitary input: rotate qubit 1 by pi*s (no reset)
        rho = R @ rho @ R.T
        rho = (P @ rho.reshape(-1, order="F")).reshape(D, D, order="F")
        feats.append([np.real(z @ np.diag(rho)) for z in Zd])
    return np.array(feats), rho
def r2(p, y):
    if np.std(p) < 1e-12: return 0.0       # constant features carry no information
    return np.corrcoef(p, y)[0, 1] ** 2
def mc(F, s, w0=100, tr=600, dmax=10):
    A = np.hstack([F, np.ones((len(F), 1))]); out = 0
    for d in range(1, dmax + 1):
        w = np.linalg.lstsq(A[w0:w0 + tr], s[w0 - d:w0 + tr - d], rcond=1e-8)[0]
        out += r2(A[w0 + tr:] @ w, s[w0 + tr - d:len(s) - d])
    return out
s = np.random.default_rng(5).uniform(0, 1, 1000)
def run_depol(s, p):
    """same unitary encoding R_y(pi s) and Hamiltonian evolution, but the only noise is global depolarising"""
    U = expm(-1j * H * 3.0); rho = np.eye(D) / D; Zd = [np.diag(op(Z, i)) for i in range(n)]; feats = []
    for x in s:
        R = op(ry(np.pi * x), 0); rho = R @ rho @ R.T
        rho = U @ rho @ U.conj().T
        rho = (1 - p) * rho + p * np.eye(D) / D
        feats.append([np.real(z @ np.diag(rho)) for z in Zd])
    return np.array(feats)
print("start from the maximally mixed state, unitary input encoding, dt = 3")
F, _ = run(s, 0.3)
print(f"  amplitude damping gamma=0.3:   MC(1..10) = {mc(F, s):.2f}, feature spread {np.std(F[100:], axis=0).max():.3f}")
for p in (0.05, 0.5):
    F = run_depol(s, p)
    print(f"  global depolarising p={p:<5}:   MC(1..10) = {mc(F, s):.2f}, feature spread {np.std(F[100:], axis=0).max():.1e}")

blocks.text: Amplitude damping gives MC $1.57$ and features that vary (spread $0.12$). Depolarising gives MC $0.00$ for both $p=0.05$ and $p=0.5$, and the features are constant to $10^{-16}$. The reason is the fixed point from the first section: the state started at $I/D$ and the combined unitary and depolarising maps all leave $I/D$ unchanged, so the input is never seen. Non-unital noise moves $I/D$ toward a state that depends on the input. In a real device with unital noise that starts the reservoir away from $I/D$ the transient does carry information, but the signal shrinks by the same factor that gives the memory, so the useful window is narrow.

blocks.title: Check yourself: depolarising memory half-life
blocks.text: A reservoir step includes a global depolarising channel with $p=0.05$. After how many steps has the trace distance between two copies halved, and what happens to $\langle Z_1\rangle=0.8$ set by the last input?
solution: Each step multiplies differences and traceless expectations by $1-p=0.95$.
$\langle Z_1\rangle$ is $0.4$ after 13.5 steps and $0.2$ after 27: memory and signal fade together.
blocks.answer: 13.5 steps; it halves on the same schedule

blocks.text: Noise on real devices

On a superconducting device the $T_1$ and $T_2$ of the qubits already supply this. Chen, Nurdin and Yamamoto ran small, noisy reservoirs on cloud-based superconducting quantum computers and solved nonlinear temporal tasks; Suzuki et al. went further and let the natural noise of the qubits supply the dissipation (natural quantum reservoir computing). Kubota et al. showed that abstract quantum noise models alone can induce useful temporal information processing, and on IBM processors found the processing capacity grew with the noise level. Which channel matters: amplitude damping, a non-unital channel, gives fading memory with an input-dependent fixed point, whereas unital noise such as depolarisation drives every state toward $I/D$ and, alone, shrinks all features toward zero together; with shot noise on top, a deep memory is unreadable.

widget.title: Two copies of a reservoir, same inputs: does the initial state wash out?

blocks.text: Try this. The plot uses the reset-injection reservoir (3 qubits by default), whose dissipation is the reset itself. (1) At the defaults the distance falls by about one decade in 40 steps (from 1 to $10^{-1.06}$): reset injection on one qubit of three contracts slowly. (2) Lower $\Delta t$ from 10 to 1: it falls only about 0.4 decades in 40 steps, because less information is carried from the untouched qubits onto the reset qubit and thrown away between resets. (3) Set $h$ to 0.01 at $\Delta t=10$: it changes little (about 0.9 decades), since the XX couplings alone still move $Z$ information onto qubit 1. (4) Switch to the classical ESN: at weight scale 0.9 the distance falls by more than five decades in 40 steps; at 1.5 it stalls near $10^{0}$ and the echo state property fails.
Choosing the dissipation

items: Match the time scale: contraction factor per step $c\approx e^{-\gamma_{\mathrm{eff}}\Delta t}$; choose $\gamma_{\mathrm{eff}}\Delta t$ so that $c^{d_{\max}}$ is around $0.1$ for the longest delay $d_{\max}$ the task needs.
Prefer non-unital channels (amplitude damping, reset) when the readout is $\langle Z\rangle$: they pull toward an input-dependent state, not toward zero.

Local dissipation on every qubit and dissipation on one qubit behave differently: a single dissipative site contracts the whole register only through the Hamiltonian, so the coupling strength and evolution time join the dissipation rate in setting the memory.
Check the echo state property numerically: run two copies from orthogonal states and confirm the distance falls below the readout's noise floor within the washout.

On hardware, decoherence varies between qubits and drifts between calibrations; a reservoir whose readout was trained last week has effectively changed. Retrain the readout, which is cheap, rather than trusting a fixed weight vector.

blocks.text: Putting it together
Problem. You have the 4-qubit amplitude-damped reservoir with $\Delta t=3$ and a task that needs delays up to 5. Choose $\gamma$, check it against the sweep, and say how long a washout you would use.

items: Step 1. Target contraction: $c^5=0.1$ gives $c=10^{-1/5}=0.631$, so $-\ln c=0.46$.
Step 2. For a single qubit the population deviation decays as $e^{-\gamma\Delta t}$, so $\gamma\Delta t=0.46$ and $\gamma=0.46/3=0.15$.

Step 3. Compare with the sweep: $\gamma=0.1$ gave MC $1.33$ and $\gamma=0.3$ gave $1.57$; the best was above the rule's value by a factor 2. The rule picks the right order of magnitude, and the best value lies higher. A plausible reason, not tested here, is that the rule uses one qubit's decay and ignores how the couplings and the readout trade memory against signal strength.

Step 4. Washout: at $\gamma=0.1$ the distance after 60 steps is $1.1\times10^{-9}$, so $c=(1.1\times10^{-9})^{1/60}=0.71$ and $10^{-6}$ is reached in about 40 steps; at $\gamma=0.03$ it needs about 96. Use at least that many, plus a margin.

blocks.text: The procedure is: set the contraction by the memory the task needs, sweep around that value, and confirm that the echo state property holds before training.
Key points

items: A unitary reservoir conserves the trace distance between states exactly, so it has no echo state property; from $I/D$ it never responds to the input at all.
Forgetting needs a non-unitary step: a reset, a measurement or environmental loss.
Per-step contraction $c$ gives a memory horizon $1/\ln(1/c)$ and a washout $N=\ln(\epsilon)/\ln c$.
Performance is non-monotonic in the loss rate: here best near $\gamma=0.3$ ($\Delta t=3$), with MC $1.57$.
Unital noise (depolarising) contracts differences and signals by the same factor and leaves $I/D$ fixed; it cannot make a reservoir work from $I/D$. Non-unital noise can.
The nonlinearity comes from the encoding and from products across steps; dissipation selects which products survive.
On hardware, retrain the readout when the noise changes.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Horizon and washout from one measurement
blocks.text: Two copies of a reservoir started in orthogonal states have trace distance $1$ at the start and $0.02$ after 30 steps. Assuming geometric contraction, find the per-step factor $c$, the memory horizon $1/\ln(1/c)$, and the washout that brings the distance to $10^{-5}$.
blocks.hint: Take the 30th root; then use $N=\ln\epsilon/\ln c$.
solution: Memory horizon: $1/0.1304=7.7$ steps: inputs older than about 8 steps are attenuated by a factor $e$ or more.
Washout: $N=\ln10^{-5}/\ln c=-11.51/-0.1304=88.3$, so discard about 90 steps.
blocks.answer: $c\approx0.878$; horizon about 7.7 steps; washout about 89 steps

blocks.title: Unital or not?
blocks.text: Apply each single-qubit channel to the maximally mixed state $I/2$ and say whether it is unital: (a) bit flip, $\rho\mapsto(1-p)\rho+pX\rho X$; (b) amplitude damping for a time with $\gamma\Delta t=0.9$; (c) reset to $\vert0\rangle$ with probability $q$, $\rho\mapsto(1-q)\rho+q\vert0\rangle\langle0\vert$. Which could make a reservoir started at $I/D$ respond to its input?
blocks.hint: Unital means $I/2\mapsto I/2$. For amplitude damping use $\langle Z\rangle(t)=1-(1-\langle Z\rangle_0)e^{-\gamma t}$ with $\langle Z\rangle_0=0$.
solution: (b) $\langle Z\rangle$ goes from 0 to $1-e^{-0.9}=1-0.407=0.593$: the state is no longer $I/2$, so the channel is not unital.

Only (b) and (c) move the state away from $I/D$, so only they (combined with an input-dependent unitary) can make a reservoir started at $I/D$ respond. A unital channel such as (a) leaves $I/D$ fixed, exactly like the depolarising channel above.
blocks.answer: (a) unital; (b) and (c) not unital, and only they can help

blocks.title: The frozen mixed state
blocks.text: A reservoir with unitary input encoding and unitary evolution starts in $\rho_0=I/D$. Show that its features never depend on the input, and name two changes that fix it.
blocks.hint: What does a unitary do to the identity?
solution: Fixes: start in a pure state (but then there is still no echo state property), or add a non-unital channel such as amplitude damping or a reset. The second fixes both problems.

blocks.title: A single qubit's relaxation per step
blocks.text: One qubit under amplitude damping with $\gamma=0.3$ is evolved for $\Delta t=3$ and starts with $\langle Z\rangle=-0.6$. What is $\langle Z\rangle$ after one step, after two steps with no new input, and what fraction of the original deviation from $+1$ remains after 5 steps?
Where this is used

The cost of reset and measurement dissipation on real hardware is the subject of Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action) and Online Measurement Protocols (#/qrc/hardware/online-protocols). The universality results that need a contractive step are in Expressivity and Universality (#/qrc/theory/expressivity-and-universality), and Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability) asks what happens to the features when the dissipation is weak and the register large.
